title: Next Greater Element II
description: Brute force to optimized: a wrapped forward scan per position versus a monotonic stack processed twice conceptually to simulate circular wrap-around.

blocks.text: Given a CIRCULAR integer array nums (the last element's next is the first element), return the next greater number for every element in nums. The next greater number of x is the first number GREATER than x when traversing the array circularly (wrapping around if necessary). If no such greater number exists anywhere in the circle, return -1 for that position.

blocks.caption: Conceptually walking the array twice (via i % n) simulates the circular wrap-around, letting the standard monotonic stack technique apply directly

blocks.text: This is exactly Next Greater Element I's core question, but applied to a SINGLE circular array: since the array wraps around, a position near the end might find its next greater value by continuing the search from the very beginning.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Next Taller Person Around a Circular Table
blocks.text: Imagine people seated around a circular table (not a straight line), and asking, for each person, who is the next taller person sitting somewhere further around the table (continuing past the last seat back to the first, if needed)? Walking around the table TWICE (conceptually) ensures that even someone seated near the "end" gets a fair chance to find a taller person sitting near the "beginning."

blocks.caption: Only pushing new stack entries during the FIRST pass avoids ever considering the same index as a candidate answer for itself during the second pass

blocks.text: Recognizing this as Next Greater Element I applied to a SINGLE circular array, the key adaptation is simulating the wrap-around by conceptually processing the array TWICE, using modular indexing, while being careful not to push duplicate index entries during the second pass.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: This is structurally identical to the standard "next greater element" monotonic stack technique, just needing to also consider positions that come "after wrapping around" from the end back to the beginning.

Observation 2: Conceptually iterating from 0 to 2n-1, but using idx = i % n to map back into the actual array indices, directly simulates walking the circular array twice, letting any position's search extend past the array's literal end.

Observation 3: During the SECOND conceptual pass (i >= n), NEW indices should NOT be pushed onto the stack again, since that would duplicate work and could incorrectly resolve an index against ITSELF; the second pass exists only to let already-pushed (from the first pass) indices find matches that appear "after wrapping."

Observation 4: Any indices STILL remaining on the stack after the full 2n iterations genuinely have no next greater element anywhere in the circle, correctly defaulting to -1.
This is the standard monotonic decreasing stack technique, extended by conceptually processing the array twice (via modular indexing) to correctly simulate circular wrap-around.
For each position, search forward up to n-1 steps (wrapping around using modular arithmetic), returning the first value found strictly greater.

items: For each index i, try up to n-1 steps forward, computing the wrapped index j = (i + step) % n at each step.
The first j found with nums[j] > nums[i] gives the answer; if none is found within n-1 steps, the answer stays -1.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Using modular arithmetic (i + step) % n directly simulates walking forward through the array while wrapping around at the end.
Limiting the search to n-1 steps prevents ever revisiting the ORIGINAL starting index itself as a candidate answer.

blocks.text: Correctly finds each position's circular next greater element, since the wrapped search directly matches the problem's definition.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2) in the worst case.
Space: O(1) extra (excluding the output).
Limitation: repeating a forward (wrapped) scan for every position is wasteful; a single monotonic stack pass, processed twice conceptually, resolves ALL positions' answers simultaneously.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rescans (with wrap-around) for every position independently. Instead, conceptually iterate from 0 to 2n-1, mapping each i to idx = i % n. Apply the standard monotonic decreasing stack technique throughout, but only PUSH new indices during the first pass (i < n); the second pass exists purely to let already-pushed indices find matches that appear after conceptually wrapping around.

Initialize a result array of -1s and an empty stack. For i from 0 to 2n-1: let idx = i % n; while the stack is non-empty and nums[stack top] < nums[idx], pop that index and set its result to nums[idx]; if i < n, push idx. Indices left on the stack after the full 2n iterations keep their default -1.
Process the array conceptually twice using modular indexing, applying the standard monotonic decreasing stack technique, but pushing new indices only during the first pass.
Dry run for nums = [1,2,1] (n=3, so i ranges 0 to 5)

codes.python:
def next_greater_elements(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    result = [-1] * n
    stack = []                                                              # a monotonic DECREASING stack of indices still awaiting their answer
    for i in range(2 * n):                                                  # conceptually walk the array TWICE, to simulate wrap-around
        idx = i % n
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < nums[idx]:                       # nums[idx] resolves everything smaller waiting on the stack
            result[stack.pop()] = nums[idx]
        if i < n:
            stack.append(idx)                                              # only PUSH new indices during the first pass (avoids duplicates)
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(next_greater_elements([1, 2, 1]))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n): the 2n conceptual iterations still bound each index to at most one push and one pop overall.
Space: O(n), for the stack and result array.

The second conceptual pass (i from n to 2n-1) lets indices that are STILL on the stack after the first pass (meaning they had not yet found a bigger value anywhere from their position to the array's literal end) get a chance to find a match by "continuing" the search from the array's beginning, exactly simulating circular wrap-around. Not pushing NEW indices during the second pass prevents any index from ever being compared against a duplicate of itself, keeping the logic correct.

items: The modulo operation (i % n) is what maps the conceptual "2n" range back onto the actual array indices, without ever physically duplicating the array itself.
The condition "if i < n: push" is the single key adaptation from the standard non-circular version, preventing incorrect duplicate pushes during the second conceptual pass.
The result array's default of -1 directly and correctly represents "no next greater element found anywhere in the circle."

blocks.text: Circular array variants of monotonic stack problems can typically be handled by conceptually processing the array TWICE using modular indexing, being careful to only push NEW candidates during the first pass, letting the second pass purely resolve wrap-around matches for candidates already pending.

items: Pushing new indices during the SECOND conceptual pass as well, which would incorrectly duplicate work and could cause an index to match against itself.
Physically duplicating the array (nums + nums) instead of using modular indexing, which works but uses unnecessary extra memory.
Forgetting the circular wrap-around entirely and applying the plain Next Greater Element I logic, which would miss valid matches that only appear after wrapping.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Next greater element, but the array is CIRCULAR" points toward the standard monotonic stack technique, adapted by conceptually processing the array twice via modular indexing.

items: Why is it safe (and correct) to only push during the FIRST pass? Because by the time the second pass begins, every index has already had its chance to be pushed; the second pass exists solely to let PENDING indices find a wrap-around match, not to introduce new candidates.

How would you adapt this for a doubly circular structure needing BOTH forward and backward wrap-around answers simultaneously? Two separate passes (or two separate stacks) would be needed, one processing the array forward for "next" and one backward for "previous," each with its own conceptual doubling.

What is the exact space savings of using modular indexing over physically duplicating the array? Avoids an extra O(n) array (nums + nums), though the stack and result array still require O(n) regardless.

A circular extension of the monotonic stack "next greater element" pattern from Next Greater Element I, using the "process twice via modular indexing" technique that generalizes to other circular-array monotonic stack problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space.
Optimized (monotonic stack, conceptual double pass): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Monotonic decreasing stack, extended for circular arrays via conceptual double-pass processing
Core Idea: Iterate from 0 to 2n-1 using idx = i % n to simulate wrap-around; only push new indices during the first pass, letting the second pass resolve pending wrap-around matches
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Pushing new indices ONLY during the first pass is what correctly prevents duplicate/self-matching work during the second, wrap-around pass
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Iterate i from 0 to 2n-1, idx=i%n, standard monotonic-stack logic, but only push when i < n
